back: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — the three core security objectives.
Disclosure, Alteration, Destruction — the negative inverse of CIA used to frame threats.
Confidentiality, Possession/Control, Integrity, Authenticity, Availability, Utility — six-attribute model expanding on CIA.
Taking the actions a reasonable person would take to protect the organisation (the 'doing').
Ongoing investigation, validation, and verification that controls remain appropriate (the 'homework').
ALE = SLE × ARO. Single Loss Expectancy times Annualised Rate of Occurrence.
SLE = AV × EF. Asset Value times Exposure Factor (the percentage of loss).
Mitigate, Avoid, Transfer (share), Accept — the four risk responses.
Inherent = risk before controls. Residual = risk remaining after controls. Secondary = risk introduced by a control.
Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege — Microsoft's threat-categorisation model.
Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability — threat-severity scoring (often paired with STRIDE).
Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis — a 7-stage, risk-centric, attacker-focused threat-modeling methodology.
Visual, Agile, Simple Threat — produces both an application threat model and an operational threat model.

term: ISC2 Code of Ethics — Canon Ordering
back: (1) Protect society, common good, public trust, infrastructure; (2) Act honourably; (3) Provide diligent service; (4) Advance the profession.
MTD = max tolerable downtime; RTO = recovery time objective; RPO = recovery point objective; WRT = work recovery time. RTO + WRT ≤ MTD.
Controller (decides purpose/means), Processor (acts on instructions), DPO (compliance/oversight), Data Subject (the individual).
Up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher) for serious violations of the regulation.
Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover (Govern was added in 2.0).
Categorise → Select → Implement → Assess → Authorise → Monitor (NIST SP 800-37).
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — contractual (not statutory) framework protecting cardholder data; v4.0 mandatory March 31, 2025.
Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002) — internal controls over financial reporting for US public companies; CEO/CFO attestations.
27001 = ISMS requirements (auditable); 27002 = control catalog/guidance.
1st: operational management; 2nd: risk/compliance; 3rd: internal audit reporting to the board.
Force absence so a substitute can detect ongoing fraud or unsafe practices that depend on continuous control by one person.
Split sensitive workflows so no single person can complete them; requires collusion to commit fraud.
Hot (minutes/hours) → Warm (~12 hours) → Cold (days) → Mobile (variable) → Reciprocal (variable).
Tabletop → Walkthrough → Simulation → Parallel → Full Interruption (least → most disruptive).
A documented risk = (threat × vulnerability × impact) with likelihood, owner, treatment, status.
Quantitative uses numbers (ALE, SLE, ARO) for cost-benefit; qualitative uses ratings (high/med/low) and captures intangibles.
Policy (mandatory intent) → Standard (mandatory specifics) → Procedure (steps) → Guideline (recommendations).
Senior business leader accountable for classification and decisions about data use, protection, and destruction.
Operational role implementing controls per owner's direction (backups, restores, ACL maintenance).
SME-style role responsible for data quality, metadata, and definitions across an organisation.
An entity that processes personal data on behalf of the controller, per controller instructions.
At rest, In transit, In use — each requires distinct protections (encryption, TLS, confidential computing).
Clear (overwrite, in-house), Purge (degauss/crypto-erase, leaves control), Destroy (shred/incinerate, highest impact).
Destroy/replace the media-encryption key on self-encrypting drives — instantly invalidates ciphertext WITHOUT touching every block.
Strong magnetic field that randomises magnetic domains — works on HDDs and tapes only (not SSDs).
Scoping REMOVES irrelevant controls. Tailoring MODIFIES remaining controls (parameters, compensating).
Low / Moderate / High impact based on confidentiality, integrity, and availability — high-water mark per dimension.
Tokenisation = substitute surrogate values, reversibility via vault. Encryption = mathematically reversible with key.
Anonymisation = irreversible, removes from GDPR scope. Pseudonymisation = reversible with separately stored key, still personal data.
Create → Store → Use → Share → Archive → Destroy.
Data Loss Prevention: detect/block sensitive data leaving authorised locations (network, endpoint, storage, email).
Confidential (damage), Secret (serious damage), Top Secret (exceptionally grave damage); FOUO is a control marking.
Public → Internal/Sensitive → Confidential → Restricted (4 tiers is generally optimal).
PII = personally identifiable information (broad). PHI = HIPAA-defined protected health information (subset, healthcare context).
Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten') — controllers must delete personal data on request unless an exemption applies.
Consent, Contract, Legal obligation, Vital interest, Public task, Legitimate interest. One of these must be cited for any processing.
End-of-Life: vendor stops selling. End-of-Support: vendor stops patching — major security risk.
Confidentiality model: NO READ UP, NO WRITE DOWN. Lattice-based, supports trusted subjects.
Integrity model: NO READ DOWN, NO WRITE UP. Inverse of Bell-LaPadula.
Integrity via well-formed transactions: subjects → TPs (transformation procedures) → CDIs/UDIs (constrained/unconstrained data items); IVPs verify integrity.
Dynamic conflict-of-interest model — restricts access based on prior access history.
Models how rights can propagate between subjects via 'take' and 'grant' operations.
Eight rules for creating/deleting subjects, objects, and rights in a protection system.
Always invoked, tamper-proof, small enough to be analysed/tested. Implemented by the security kernel.
Trusted Computing Base — hardware/software/firmware whose correctness is essential to security policy enforcement.
Evaluation Assurance Level (EAL1 functionally tested → EAL7 formally verified). Measures evaluation rigor, NOT inherent security.
Federal validation standard for cryptographic modules; four levels; references ISO/IEC 19790:2012.
ECB (insecure-deterministic), CBC (chaining, no integrity), CTR (stream-like), GCM (AEAD: confidentiality + integrity).
Symmetric: shared key (fast, key distribution problem). Asymmetric: keypair (slower, solves distribution; identity binding via PKI).
One-way (irreversible), collision-resistant, fixed-length output, deterministic. Examples: SHA-256, SHA-3.
Hash + private-key encryption. Provides integrity + authenticity + non-repudiation. MACs lack non-repudiation.
CA (issues), RA (registers), CRL/OCSP (revokes), repository (stores). Hierarchical or web-of-trust.
Trusted Platform Module — chip on the motherboard providing root of trust for measurement, sealed storage, attestation.
Hardware Security Module — tamper-resistant appliance for high-volume key generation, storage, and crypto operations.
Recover secrets from observable physical phenomena (power, EM, timing, acoustic) during processing.
Storage: signal via shared resource state. Timing: signal via varying access timings. Both are unintentional disclosure paths.
A: ordinary combustibles (water). B: flammable liquids/gas. C: electrical (no water!). D: combustible metals. K: cooking oils.
Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design: natural surveillance, natural access control, territorial reinforcement.
Least privilege, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least common mechanism, psychological acceptability, economy of mechanism.
ASLR = randomise memory layout; DEP/NX = mark data pages non-executable. Combined OS hardening against memory-corruption exploits.
FIPS 203 ML-KEM (Kyber), 204 ML-DSA (Dilithium), 205 SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) — first post-quantum standards.
Perfect Forward Secrecy: compromise of long-term key cannot decrypt PAST sessions. Achieved via ephemeral key exchange (DHE/ECDHE).
Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Mnemonic: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away'.
Link, Internet, Transport, Application — collapsed alternative to OSI used in practice.
Mandates forward secrecy, removes RSA key transport, AEAD ciphers only, faster handshake (1-RTT, 0-RTT optional).
AH: integrity over IP header + payload (no confidentiality, BREAKS through NAT). ESP: payload confidentiality + integrity (NAT-T uses UDP/4500).
Transport: protect payload, original IP header visible (host-to-host). Tunnel: encapsulate full packet (gateway-to-gateway).
DNS Security Extensions — cryptographic origin authentication and integrity for DNS responses (NOT confidentiality).
DoH: DNS over HTTPS (port 443; blends with web traffic; harder for enterprise inspection). DoT: DNS over TLS (port 853; visible to enterprise).
WPA3 uses SAE (Dragonfly) handshake, defeating offline dictionary attacks against captured handshakes; provides forward secrecy per session.
EAP-TLS (mutual cert), PEAP (server cert + tunnel), EAP-TTLS (server cert + flexible inner), EAP-FAST (PAC). EAP-MD5 obsolete.
Stateful tracks connections. NGFW adds application identification, integrated IPS, threat intelligence.
Web Application Firewall — L7-specific, rules for SQLi/XSS/etc; OWASP Core Rule Set is common.
Assume the network is hostile; verify identity, device posture, context per request; least-privilege access per resource (NIST SP 800-207).
Fine-grained workload-to-workload policy controls limiting east-west lateral movement after compromise.
Software-Defined Networking — decouples control plane from data plane; centralised programmatic control; controller is a SPOF.
Virtual Extensible LAN — extends L2 over L3 underlay using UDP encapsulation; does NOT provide encryption by default.
ARP spoofing (L2), DNS poisoning, MAC flooding, Smurf (ICMP amplification), Fraggle (UDP), Teardrop (overlapping fragments), Ping of Death.
Isolated network segment for internet-facing services, separated from internal network by firewall(s).
Site-to-site (IPsec, gateway-to-gateway), Remote-access (IPsec or SSL/TLS clientless), modern: WireGuard.
SPF (authorised IPs), DKIM (signed headers), DMARC (alignment + policy + reporting). All three together.
S/MIME = end-to-end content encryption + signature. SPF/DKIM/DMARC = envelope-level anti-spoofing.
IDS: detect + alert (passive). IPS: detect + actively block (inline). Performance and false-positive risk are higher for IPS.
Volumetric (saturate bandwidth), Protocol (SYN flood), Application-layer (Slowloris, HTTP flood), Reflective amplification (DNS/NTP/memcached).
Zero Trust Network Access — broker per-application access by identity/context without exposing broad network ranges.
Time sync is critical for log correlation, Kerberos ticket validity, certificate validation, and forensic timelines.
Identification, Authentication, Authorisation, Accounting (auditing) — the four-step access control flow.
Something you know (password), Something you have (token), Something you are (biometric), sometimes Somewhere you are (location).
Discretionary Access Control — owner grants access at their discretion (file-system ACLs).
Mandatory Access Control — system enforces clearance + label policy; appropriate for classified environments.
Role-Based Access Control — permissions tied to roles; users inherit permissions through role membership.
Attribute-Based Access Control — decisions based on user, resource, action, environment attributes (e.g., XACML, AWS IAM, Azure Conditional Access).
System-wide rules apply uniformly regardless of identity (e.g., firewall ACLs).
AS (authentication server), TGS (ticket-granting server), KDC (encompassing AS+TGS), TGT, service ticket, principal.
Tickets time-bound; clock skew tolerance ~5 minutes default. NTP is operationally critical.
Kerberoasting (offline-crack service-ticket ciphertext), Pass-the-Hash (NTLM), Golden Ticket (forge TGTs from KRBTGT), Silver Ticket (forge service tickets).
XML-based federation. IdP authenticates and issues an assertion (authentication, attribute, authorisation) to the SP.
Delegated AUTHORISATION framework — issues access tokens to third-party apps. NOT authentication on its own.
Authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0; ID token is a JWT carrying identity claims.
JSON Web Token — compact, URL-safe, signed (JWS) and optionally encrypted (JWE) token format.
RADIUS: UDP, password-only encryption, AuthN+AuthZ combined. TACACS+: TCP, full payload encryption, separated AAA, supports per-command auth.
Hardware-backed cryptographic authenticator providing AAL3 verifier-impersonation resistance per NIST 800-63B.
No mandatory composition rules, no routine forced expiration, ≥8 chars, check against breached-password corpus, support up to 64 chars.
Just-In-Time access — grant privileges only when needed, time-limited; eliminates standing privilege.
Privileged Access Management — vault credentials, broker sessions with recording, MFA, automatic rotation.
FAR (false acceptance — security failure), FRR (false rejection — usability failure). CER/EER = crossover where they meet (lower is better).
System for Cross-domain Identity Management — standard for provisioning users between IdP and SaaS providers.
Accumulating rights as roles change without removing old permissions; mitigated by access reviews and HR-driven deprovisioning.
Time-based / HMAC-based OTP — RFC 6238 / RFC 4226. Authenticator app generates, verifier checks locally.
AAL1 (single-factor), AAL2 (two-factor with replay resistance), AAL3 (hardware crypto, verifier-impersonation resistant — FIDO2).
Static Application Security Testing — analyse source/bytecode without execution. White-box. Finds patterns like SQLi, hardcoded secrets.
Dynamic Application Security Testing — exercise running app from outside. Black-box. Finds runtime-manifest issues.
Interactive AST — agent inside running app combines source visibility with runtime context.
Send malformed/unexpected inputs to surface input-handling defects (crashes, memory errors, parser bugs).
Planning, Discovery, Attack, Reporting (4 phases). PTES defines 7.
Black (no info — external attacker), Gray (partial info — insider), White (full info — insider with everything).
SOC 1: financial-reporting controls (ISAE 3402 equivalent). SOC 2: Trust Services Criteria. SOC 3: SOC 2 public summary.

term: SOC 2 Type I vs Type II
back: Type I: design at point-in-time. Type II: design + operating effectiveness over period (typically 6-12 months). Type II preferred by relying parties.
Scans identify potential weaknesses (breadth). Pen tests exploit them to demonstrate impact (depth).
Authenticated logs in to reveal host-level patches/configs. Unauthenticated sees only externally exposed surfaces.
KPI: performance metric (mean time to patch). KRI: risk-exposure metric (count of overdue critical vulnerabilities).
Security Information and Event Management — correlate cross-source events to detect attacks; produces alerts.
Security Orchestration, Automation, Response — playbook automation across tools (containment, enrichment, ticketing).
Red: offensive. Blue: defensive. Purple: collaborative — share red techniques to improve blue detection/response.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System — 0-10 severity (Base, Temporal, Environmental). Current v4.0.
Knowledge base of adversary tactics (TA), techniques (T), and procedures used in real attacks; standard for detection engineering.
Breach and Attack Simulation — automated execution of attacker techniques to validate detection/prevention controls continuously.
Scripted requests simulating user actions to monitor availability and correctness.
Manual peer review excels at logic/business-rule defects automated SAST misses; combine both.
Signed authorisation letter + rules of engagement before starting — without it, the test is unauthorised intrusion.
Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment, Eradication & Recovery → Post-Incident Activity.
CPU registers/cache → System memory → Network state → Disk → Remote logs → Backup tapes (most → least volatile).
Documented record of evidence from collection through court — every transfer, location, access logged. Required for admissibility.
Best (original/primary), Secondary (copies), Hearsay (out-of-court statement), Demonstrative (charts/models), Circumstantial.
Stripe across drives — performance boost, NO redundancy.
Mirror — identical copies on two drives, survives one failure, 50% storage efficiency.
Stripe with distributed parity — survives one failure, write penalty.
Stripe with dual parity — survives TWO simultaneous failures.
Mirror then stripe — fast and resilient; survives multiple failures if not in same mirror pair.
Fully equipped, near-real-time data, ready in minutes/hours; highest cost, lowest RTO.
Hardware ready, stale data, ~12-hour activation. Mid cost / mid RTO.
Space and utilities only; equipment + data must be brought in. Cheapest, longest RTO.
Trailer with equipment driven to needed location.
Mutual aid pact between organisations — cheap but problematic (capacity, regional disasters, confidentiality).
Full (everything), Differential (since last full — slower backup, faster restore), Incremental (since last backup — faster backup, slower restore).
3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite. Modern variants add immutability (3-2-1-1-0).
MTBF: Mean Time Between Failures — reliability. MTTR: Mean Time To Repair — recoverability. Lower MTTR is better.
Body that authorises changes balancing risk, business impact, security. Emergency CAB (eCAB) handles urgent changes.
EDR provides continuous endpoint telemetry, behavioural detection, response (isolate/kill/retrieve), and forensic data — beyond static AV.
User & Entity Behaviour Analytics — baselines normal behaviour, alerts on deviations (impossible travel, unusual data access).
Decoy system to attract, detect, and study attackers. Honeynet = whole network of decoys.
Civil: preponderance (>50%). Criminal: beyond reasonable doubt. Administrative: clear and convincing. Warrants: probable cause.
Restrict access by job-justified need, even when general clearance/role allows broader access.
Threshold below which monitoring suppresses alerts to reduce noise (e.g., ignore <5 failed logins).
Linear SDLC — requirements → design → implementation → testing → deployment. No phase backtracking.
Iterative SDLC — short cycles, customer feedback, working software each iteration (Scrum, Kanban, XP).
Risk-driven iterative SDLC — each cycle includes risk assessment.
Security embedded continuously across CI/CD with automation (SAST, DAST, SCA, IaC scan, secrets detection).
Capability Maturity Model Integration — five process maturity levels: Initial → Managed → Defined → Quantitatively Managed → Optimising.
Prescriptive software-security maturity framework: Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification, Operations × four levels.
Descriptive maturity model based on observed activities at member organisations (not prescriptive).
A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Cryptographic Failures, A03 Injection, A04 Insecure Design, A06 Vulnerable Components, A10 SSRF.
Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use race condition — state changes between authorisation check and use (CWE-367).
Memory-safe languages (Rust, Go); bounds checking; ASLR + DEP/NX; stack canaries; safer APIs (snprintf vs strcpy).
Parameterised queries / prepared statements treat input as data, not code — structurally prevents injection.
Context-aware output encoding (HTML body vs attribute vs JS) plus a strict Content Security Policy.
Anti-CSRF tokens (synchroniser pattern) + SameSite cookies (Lax/Strict).
Allow-list destinations, block private/metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), use a controlled egress proxy.
Database transaction properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
Combine individually authorised queries to deduce unauthorised information.
Combining individually low-classification data into a higher-classification whole.
Multiple records with the same primary key at different security levels — defends against inference via existence.
Software Bill of Materials — structured component inventory (SPDX or CycloneDX). Required by US EO 14028.
Software Composition Analysis — scan dependencies for known CVEs and licence issues.
Secure Software Development Framework: Prepare the Org, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software, Respond to Vulnerabilities.
Application Security Verification Standard — three verification levels (1-3) of security requirements.
Embed privacy from inception — minimisation, purpose limitation, default-private, transparency. Codified in GDPR Article 25.
Service-to-service: OAuth 2.0 client_credentials with short-lived tokens, or mTLS for workload identity.
